gap: The paper archives more than one certificate for the 16-element bounds (a 329-function and a 365-function depth-28 certificate, and a 252-function depth-29 certificate for rank 8); it does not say which is canonical for verification.
options: Use the 329-function certificate listed in Table 3 (SHA-256 prefix eb8f064c12bb)
Use the alternative 365-function certificate
Verify both
chosen: Verify the 329-function certificate from Table 3, and optionally the 365-function one as a second witness
rationale: Table 3 lists SHA-256 prefixes for the certificates used in the Lean proofs, so the 329-function file is the one whose hash is pinned and whose Lean theorem is named.
quote: Further certificates for the 16-element bounds, with 365 and 252 functions, are archived.

gap: The certificate file format is only described as 'Rust programs in the format of the search code of [5]'; the accepted grammar of the static checker is not specified in the paper.
options: Use the archived Rust files and the shipped checker verbatim
Re-implement the grammar from Section 3.1's example
Translate to a new format and re-verify
chosen: Use the archived Rust certificate files and the archived checker/parser unchanged
rationale: Any re-implementation of the grammar is an independent source of divergence; the archived pair is the object the Lean proof and SHA-256 hashes refer to.
quote: Our certificates are such graphs, written as Rust programs in the format of the search code of [5].

gap: Theorem 1's equality V7(16) = 28 needs the lower bound V7(16) ≥ 28, which the paper imports rather than derives.
options: Report only the upper bound V7(16) ≤ 28 as this paper's result
Import the lower bound from [5, Table 3] entry 28–33
Re-derive the lower bound
chosen: Report V7(16) ≤ 28 as reproduced and take V7(16) ≥ 28 from [5] to state the equality
rationale: The paper states explicitly that it uses the lower bound without rederiving it, so a faithful reproduction of this paper alone cannot establish the equality.
quote: The lower bound of Theorem 1 is the entry 28–33 of [5, Table 3], obtained there by computer search; we use it without rederiving it.

gap: Two rank conventions coexist: Vi(n) is 1-based (V7 = 7th smallest) while certificates declare a 0-based rank, so the target triple is (n, r) = (16, 6).
options: Use 0-based r = i − 1 internally and report 1-based Vi(n)
Use 1-based rank throughout
chosen: Internal/certificate ranks are 0-based (r = 6 for the 7th smallest); all reported V values are 1-based
rationale: Every checker rule (m − r successors, r + 1 predecessors) and every Lean triple (16, 6, 28) uses the 0-based convention.
quote: A doc comment declares the size, the 0-based rank, and known relations.

gap: The df-pn cost predictor, its pessimistic shift and the initialization of unexplored nodes are not specified numerically, so regenerating the certificate from scratch is under-determined.
options: Re-run df-pn with a predictor refitted to a self-generated corpus
Skip search and verify the archived certificate
Tune the shift until budget 28 for (16, 7) is solved quickly
chosen: Skip certificate search; verify the archived 329-function certificate. If search must be reproduced, fit the predictor to a self-collected corpus of solved small instances.
rationale: The paper states the heuristics need not be correct for the results to hold; only the certificate matters for the theorem.
quote: We initialize unexplored nodes from a cost predictor fitted to the corpus of solved small problems, shifted pessimistically, which mattered by factors of 10–100.

gap: The cost model for known-outcome comparisons: the Lean lower-bound development allows comparing already-ordered elements, while the checker rejects them; which is normative for a certificate.
options: Forbid comparing elements whose order is already implied (checker rule 1)
Allow them and let the counter count them anyway
chosen: Forbid redundant comparisons in produced certificates (checker rule 1), while noting soundness does not require it
rationale: Rule 1 is part of the accepted grammar; certificates that compare known-ordered pairs would be rejected even though they might be sound.
quote: compared elements are incomparable before the comparison (this rejects wasted comparisons; soundness does not need it)

gap: The pseudorandom permutation generator and seed used for the 2·10^7 compiled executions are not stated.
options: Uniform random permutations from a fixed seeded PRNG
All permutations for small n plus random for n = 16, 17
chosen: Uniform random permutations of 0..n−1 from a fixed documented seed, 2·10^7 draws per certificate
rationale: This test is a sanity check on top of the proof, not part of the bound; any fixed seed reproduces the intent.
quote: Each certificate also passes 2 · 107 compiled executions on pseudorandom permutations.

gap: The Lean 4 toolchain version and (for the lower-bound development) the Mathlib pin are not given; only the axiom set and leanchecker replay are stated.
options: Use the version pinned by the archived repository
Use the latest Lean 4 release
chosen: Use whatever Lean/Mathlib versions the archived repository pins
rationale: Kernel evaluation of the checker on certificate data is version-sensitive; the archive is the only pinned source.
quote: It uses only Lean’s core library, so every definition the theorems depend on is contained in our own short specification.

gap: Search wall-clock times are machine-specific and single-thread; the paper reports times but the hardware is only named, not benchmarked.
options: Report times on the stated hardware (AMD Ryzen 7 5800X, single thread)
Report only that a certificate of the stated depth was found/verified
chosen: Treat search time as informational; the acceptance criterion is the certificate's verified depth
rationale: Times in Table 3/4 vary by machine and by heuristic tuning; they are not part of any theorem.
quote: found by proof-number search (single thread, AMD Ryzen 7 5800X)

gap: The input domain: elements are distinct and only their relative order matters, but the paper does not spell out the reduction used in testing.
options: Test on permutations of 0..n−1 (ranks)
Test on arbitrary distinct integers/reals
chosen: Test on permutations of 0..n−1; the certificate accesses inputs only by comparison, so this is without loss of generality
rationale: The paper argues that replacing n distinct elements of any totally ordered set by their ranks leaves every execution unchanged, which cleanly separates the certificate from the input representation.
quote: replacing n distinct elements of any totally ordered set by their ranks 0, . . . , n −1 leaves every execution unchanged
